core.text: Put the gerundive (the '-nd-' adjective: 'to be done'; aqua bibenda = water to be drunk) next to a form of *sum* (to be) and you get **the gerundive with sum (the 'must be done' pattern: liber legendus est = the book must be read)**. *Cibus comedendus est* — the food must be eaten; *tacendum est* — one must be silent (no subject, so the neuter *-um*). Latin name: *coniugātiō periphrastica passīva*.
English: *the food is to be eaten*, *it must be eaten*. Think 'has to be done', then say it naturally: *we have to eat the food*.
Gerundive agreeing with the subject + sum = must / ought to be; neuter -ndum est with no subject = one must; in reported speech -ndum esse.

invented.en: The letter must be written today.

core.text: *laudātus est* — the perfect passive (the 'was done / has been done' form: laudatus est), he was praised — and *laudandus est* (he must be praised) share the shape participle + *est*. Look at the participle: *-tus / -sus* is the perfect passive participle (done); *-ndus* is the gerundive, to be done. *victus est* = was beaten; *vincendus est* = must be beaten.

more.text: The tense of *sum* moves the duty in time: *pūniendus erat* — had to be punished. The person who must do it is added in the dative (the 'to/for' form), not with ā/ab: *liber mihi legendus est* — I must read the book. See the dative of agent lesson.

The learner's notes: the future passive participle is commonly joined with a form of *sum* to make a short sentence about what needs to be done (*aqua bibenda est*, the water needs drinking), and just as often sits inside an accusative + infinitive clause with *esse*: *sciō cibum comedendum esse* — I know the food needs eating; *intellegis vōcem audiendam esse*.

Ørberg's chapter 31: *discipulus industrius magistrō laudandus est; discipulus piger reprehendendus et pūniendus est; tacendum est; Lingua Latīna vōbīs discenda est; quidquid magister imperāvit discipulō faciendum est; dominus dīcit ovēs bene cūrandās esse.* With a verb that takes no object the pattern is always the impersonal neuter: *eundum est* (one must go), *pugnandum est*, *dēspērandum nōn est*. The Latin name means 'the roundabout passive conjugation'; Cato's *Carthāgō dēlenda est* (Carthage must be destroyed) is the famous case.
